questions.text: Vault door openings for nitro-cellulose film storage must be of what minimum fire-resistive construction rating per PD 1096, Rule XIV (Sec. 1401)?

options.text: 2-hour fire-resistive
3-hour fire-resistive
4-hour fire-resistive
1-hour fire-resistive

questions.rationale: Sec. 1401 requires vault door openings to be of 4-hour fire-resistive construction — the highest standard prescribed under PD 1096. This is the same rating applied to the most critical fire separations in the Code. Vault doors must be kept closed except when in use; a propped-open 4-hour door provides zero protection. This requirement is identical to NFPA 40.

questions.text: According to the PFMEC mnemonic for PD 1096 Rule VI, Sec. 603, what does each letter stand for in the five assembly categories?

options.text: P = Partitions, F = Foundations, M = Masonry, E = Exterior, C = Columns, covering the basic structural elements

P = Partitions (solid concrete, solid masonry, hollow unit masonry), F = Floors (RC slab, prestressed concrete), M = Metal protection (concrete, masonry, plaster), E = Exterior walls (solid concrete, solid masonry, hollow masonry), C = Columns (RC, all faces exposed)
P = Plaster systems, F = Fire-resistive ratings, M = Metal columns, E = Encasement, C = Concrete, focusing on fire safety and structural integrity
P = Protection for metal, F = Floors, M = Masonry partitions, E = Exterior insulation, C = Concrete columns, emphasizing thermal and structural protection

questions.rationale: Use PFMEC when an exam question asks which category a specific assembly belongs to, or when verifying you have covered all five categories in a compliance checklist.

questions.text: What is the minimum cover to tendons for a prestressed concrete slab achieving a 4-hour fire resistance rating under PD 1096 Rule VI, Sec. 603, and how does it compare to ordinary RC cover at the same rating?

options.text: 25 mm; ordinary RC also requires 25 mm at 4 hours — both are the same
65 mm; this is 2.6× more than ordinary RC's 25 mm at 4 hours
50 mm; this is twice ordinary RC's 25 mm at 4 hours
65 mm; this is approximately the same as ordinary RC's 65 mm at 4 hours

questions.rationale: The growing ratio of prestressed to RC cover (1.67 at 1 hr → 2.0 at 2-3 hr → 2.6 at 4 hr) reflects the disproportionately greater temperature sensitivity of high-strength prestressing steel at extreme fire exposure durations.

questions.text: A structural engineer proposes an RC column with a minimum cross-sectional dimension of 300 mm (all faces exposed) for a building in a Highly Fire Restrictive Zone requiring four-hour fire-resistive construction throughout. Is this column dimensionally compliant with PD 1096 Rule VI?

options.text: Yes — 300 mm exceeds the 200 mm minimum for 1-hour fire resistance and is adequate for a multi-hour rating
No — a four-hour rating for RC columns (all faces exposed) requires a minimum dimension of 450 mm per Sec. 603
Yes — 300 mm satisfies the two-hour fire resistance requirement, which is sufficient for exterior elements of a Fire Restrictive Zone
No — RC columns are not permitted in Highly Fire Restrictive Zones; only steel columns with masonry encasement qualify

questions.rationale: The RC column progression (PFMEC mnemonic: 'Two-Five-Zero, Add a Hundred, Then Slow Down') is: 1 hr → 200 mm, 2 hr → 300 mm, 3 hr → 400 mm, 4 hr → 450 mm. The 4-hour value breaks the +100 pattern at +50.

questions.text: A Type V building (4-hour fire-resistive construction) uses exposed RC columns. What is the minimum column dimension per Sec. 603, and what is the minimum thickness of metal lath with vermiculite plaster required for exposed steel beams per Sec. 603?

options.text: Column: 450 mm; Steel beam protection: 50 mm
Column: 400 mm; Steel beam protection: 75 mm
Column: 450 mm; Steel beam protection: 100 mm
Column: 300 mm; Steel beam protection: 50 mm

questions.rationale: Type V buildings require 4-hour rating throughout. The 450 mm RC column and 50 mm plaster protection represent the most stringent requirements in the Sec. 603 table for their respective categories.

questions.text: An RC floor slab has a cover to reinforcement of 25 mm and an overall depth of 125 mm. What is the maximum fire-resistance time period rating of this assembly under PD 1096 Rule VI, Sec. 603?

options.text: 4 hours — 25 mm cover exceeds the 3-hour and 4-hour cover requirement, which is a common misunderstanding
2 hours — 125 mm depth satisfies the 2-hour depth requirement; 25 mm cover exceeds it, so the more limiting criterion (depth) governs
3 hours — 125 mm depth satisfies the 3-hour requirement and 25 mm cover exceeds the 3-hour cover requirement, which is often misinterpreted
1 hour — the assembly's overall depth of 125 mm is insufficient for any rating above 1 hour, which is a misconception

questions.rationale: This is the most critical exam trap in Sec. 603. Both sub-requirements (cover AND depth) must be satisfied simultaneously. The achievable rating is always the LOWER of the two individual ratings — not the higher.

questions.text: An architect must select a fire protection system for exposed structural steel beams in a 4-hour fire-resistive assembly (Type V construction). According to PD 1096 Rule VI, Sec. 603, which system achieves the 4-hour rating at the minimum thickness?

options.text: Concrete encasement at 75 mm — the densest material provides the best protection at minimum thickness, though it may add significant weight to the structure
Solid masonry encasement at 100 mm — masonry is the most durable and robust option, but requires additional structural support
Metal lath with vermiculite/perlite gypsum plaster at 50 mm — the most thermally efficient system achieves 4-hour rating at minimum thickness
All three systems achieve the 4-hour rating at the same thickness since they are all tested to the same performance standard, though practical application may vary

questions.rationale: The material efficiency hierarchy for metal protection: plaster (thinnest) → concrete → masonry (thickest). Thermal efficiency is determined by microstructural void geometry, not bulk density. Vermiculite/perlite's microscopic pores create superior insulation at minimal thickness.

questions.text: What is the minimum thickness for a solid concrete exterior wall achieving a 2-hour fire resistance rating under PD 1096 Rule VI, Sec. 603?

options.text: 100 mm
125 mm
150 mm
180 mm

questions.rationale: Compare to partitions: solid concrete partition at 2 hours = 150 mm vs. solid concrete exterior wall at 2 hours = 125 mm. The difference narrows at higher ratings (175 mm vs. 180 mm at 4 hours) because thermal mass dominates.

questions.text: Under PD 1096 Rule VI, what does Sec. 601 define, and what does Sec. 602 define?

options.text: Sec. 601 defines fire-resistive rating (degree — the concept); Sec. 602 defines fire-resistive time period rating (hours — the unit of measurement)
Sec. 601 defines fire-resistive time period rating (hours); Sec. 602 defines fire-resistive rating (degree), with additional guidelines for implementation
Both sections define fire-resistive rating; Sec. 602 adds specific test methods, including those for different material types
Sec. 601 defines material classifications; Sec. 602 defines fire testing protocols, ensuring compliance with international standards

questions.rationale: This is a definitions test. Sec. 601 = 'what it is' (degree/performance). Sec. 602 = 'how it's measured' (time period in hours). These are two separate definitional sections intentionally separated in the Code.

questions.text: A solid prestressed concrete floor slab has 40 mm of cover to the prestressing tendons and an overall depth of 125 mm. What is the maximum fire-resistance time period rating this assembly can achieve under PD 1096 Rule VI, Sec. 603?

options.text: 4 hours — 40 mm cover significantly exceeds the 1-hour minimum of 25 mm, providing enhanced protection
3 hours — 40 mm cover to tendons meets the 3-hour cover requirement for prestressed concrete, ensuring compliance with fire safety standards
2 hours — 40 mm cover satisfies the 2-hour cover requirement; the 125 mm overall depth satisfies the 2-hour depth requirement; both criteria are met
1 hour — prestressed concrete always requires significantly greater protection than ordinary RC, making 40 mm cover marginal, especially in high-risk areas

questions.rationale: This tests the 'more limiting criterion' rule: both sub-requirements (cover AND depth) must be satisfied simultaneously. The achievable rating is always the lower of the two individual ratings.

questions.text: Per PD 1096 Rule VI, Sec. 603, what is the material efficiency hierarchy for protecting metal structural members, from thinnest to thickest?

options.text: Masonry encasement → Concrete encasement → Metal lath with vermiculite/perlite gypsum plaster
Metal lath with vermiculite/perlite gypsum plaster → Concrete encasement → Masonry encasement
Concrete encasement → Metal lath with vermiculite/perlite gypsum plaster → Masonry encasement
All three systems have the same minimum thickness at equivalent fire resistance ratings

questions.rationale: This hierarchy guides material selection: plaster for space-constrained/high-rise steel frames (lightest, thinnest); concrete for robust columns; masonry where permanence and robustness outweigh thickness penalty.

questions.text: What is the minimum thickness of metal lath with vermiculite/perlite gypsum plaster required to achieve a 1-hour fire resistance rating for metal structural members under PD 1096 Rule VI, Sec. 603?

options.text: 12 mm
20 mm
38 mm
50 mm

questions.rationale: Modern spray-applied fire-resistive materials (SFRM) are the contemporary successors to traditional vermiculite plaster. At 12 mm for 1-hour protection, they are the most material-efficient system in the table.

questions.text: What is the minimum cover to reinforcement for a reinforced concrete slab achieving a 2-hour fire resistance rating under PD 1096 Rule VI, Sec. 603?

options.text: 15 mm
20 mm
25 mm
30 mm

questions.rationale: The RC slab cover progression mirrors the fire-resistive time investment: more cover = more thermal protection = longer time before steel reaches critical temperature (~600°C).

questions.text: What is the minimum thickness for a hollow unit masonry partition achieving a 4-hour fire resistance rating under PD 1096 Rule VI, Sec. 603?

options.text: 200 mm
250 mm
300 mm
175 mm

questions.rationale: The hollow masonry vs. solid concrete comparison at 4 hours: 300 mm vs. 175 mm (71% more thickness). This is the most dramatic material difference in the entire table.

questions.text: What is the minimum thickness for a solid concrete partition achieving a 4-hour fire resistance rating under PD 1096 Rule VI, Sec. 603?

options.text: 150 mm
175 mm
200 mm
125 mm

questions.rationale: Solid concrete partitions and RC floor slabs share the same 175 mm / 3-4 hr threshold because both use dense, homogeneous concrete thermal mass.

questions.text: What is the minimum overall depth for a reinforced concrete floor slab achieving a 2-hour fire resistance rating under PD 1096 Rule VI, Sec. 603?

options.text: 100 mm
125 mm
150 mm
200 mm

questions.rationale: The overall depth requirements for RC slabs match exactly between prestressed and ordinary RC at all ratings: 1 hr = 100 mm, 2 hr = 125 mm, 3-4 hr = 150 mm.

questions.text: What is the minimum thickness of Type X gypsum board used in fire-resistive assemblies under PD 1096 Rule XII, Sec. 1215, and what fire-resistance rating can it contribute to in a complete tested assembly?

options.text: 9.5 mm Type X board; contributes to a 1-hour fire-resistance rating in a complete tested assembly
12.7 mm (1/2 inch) Type X board; contributes to a 1-hour fire-resistance rating in a complete tested assembly
15.9 mm (5/8 inch) Type X board; contributes to a 1-hour fire-resistance rating in a complete tested assembly
15.9 mm (5/8 inch) Type X board; contributes to a 2-hour fire-resistance rating in a complete tested assembly

questions.rationale: The critical principle: no single product achieves a fire-resistance rating in isolation. Type X board achieves 1-hour rating only as part of a complete tested assembly: correct stud size/spacing, fastener pattern, joint treatment, and any required insulation. Deviation voids the rating.

questions.text: Why does a Type X gypsum board achieve a fire-resistance rating only as part of a complete tested assembly, not as a standalone product specification?

options.text: Because gypsum board manufacturers require a complete assembly to validate their product warranty, ensuring compliance with industry standards
Because fire-resistance rating is a function of the complete assembly — including stud size and spacing, fastener pattern, joint treatment, and insulation — not the board product alone
Because Type X gypsum board is only manufactured to be used with metal studs, not wood studs, limiting its application
Because the fire test (ASTM E119) cannot test individual board products, only full wall assemblies, ensuring comprehensive safety evaluation

questions.rationale: This is Principle 3 of Sec. 1215: 'It is an assembly, not a single product.' An architect specifying Type X board must also specify the complete assembly — stud size, spacing, fastener pattern, joint treatment — or the rating is not achieved.

questions.text: Under PD 1096 Rule XII, Sec. 1215, which wall board specification would be appropriate for a corridor wall in a Type V (fire-resistive) building requiring a 2-hour fire-resistive partition rating?

options.text: 9.5 mm regular gypsum board on steel studs — adequate for any corridor in a Type V building, although not meeting the 2-hour fire-resistive requirement
Metal lath with 3-coat Portland cement plaster (rated assembly) or Type X gypsum board in a tested 2-hour assembly
Moisture-resistant gypsum board at 12.7 mm — the moisture resistance provides fire resistance, which is a common misconception
Wood lath with 3-coat gypsum plaster — wood lath is permitted in fire-resistive construction, but not suitable for 2-hour fire-resistive partitions

questions.rationale: This tests the FLAT-CF framework: F (fire rating = 2-hour) + T (Type V = incombustible) + A (rated assembly required) = metal lath + plaster or Type X in tested 2-hour assembly.

questions.text: Under PD 1096 Rule XII, Sec. 1215, which material is the most thermally efficient for protecting structural steel members and achieves fire-resistance ratings at the thinnest profile?

options.text: Masonry encasement — its density and mass provide the best thermal insulation for steel members, although it may require additional structural support.
Metal lath with vermiculite/perlite gypsum plaster — the microscopic void structure of vermiculite and perlite creates excellent thermal insulation at minimal thickness
Concrete encasement — its thermal mass provides superior fire protection compared to plaster systems, but it is heavier and may affect structural load calculations.
All protection systems achieve equivalent fire-resistance ratings at the same thickness, making material choice a matter of cost and availability.

questions.rationale: This connects Sec. 1215 to Rule VI, Sec. 603 (Metal Protection Category). Metal lath + vermiculite plaster achieves 1-hour at 12 mm, 2-hour at 20 mm, 3-hour at 38 mm, 4-hour at 50 mm — thinner than any other system at equivalent ratings.

questions.text: Using the FLAT-CF mnemonic for wall board selection under PD 1096 Rule XII, Sec. 1215, what does each letter stand for?

options.text: F = Fire rating, L = Load capacity, A = Assembly type, T = Thickness, C = Construction type, F = Floor area, which are all critical for compliance

F = Fire-resistive rating required, L = Location (interior/exterior), A = Assembly (tested/rated or non-rated), T = Type of construction, C = Code reference (Rule VI/RA 9514), F = Finish (flame-spread requirements)
F = Finish material, L = Lathing type, A = Application method, T = Thickness requirement, C = Combustibility class, F = Fire-resistance duration, ensuring safety and durability
F = Fastening pattern, L = Load-bearing capacity, A = Adhesive type, T = Thermal resistance, C = Climate zone, F = Fastener spacing, which are essential for structural integrity

questions.rationale: FLAT-CF is the systematic decision framework for lath and plaster specification. Sec. 1215 is not standalone — it connects Rule IV (construction type), Rule VI (fire-resistive ratings), and RA 9514 (flame-spread) into one decision sequence.

questions.text: What is the KEY structural distinction between Type II and Type III construction in PD 1096?

options.text: Type II uses masonry throughout; Type III allows wood framing, which affects fire resistance
Both are approximately 1-hour fire-resistive, but Type III requires incombustible exterior walls
Type II is fire-resistive throughout; Type III allows unprotected wood exterior, which is less fire-resistant
Type II is for commercial buildings; Type III is for residential buildings, which is a common misconception

questions.rationale: The exterior wall requirement is what separates Type II from Type III — both rate approximately 1-hour, but Type III's incombustible exterior walls provide better protection against external fire spread.

questions.text: What type of construction is Type IV classified as under PD 1096?

options.text: Wood construction with fire-resistive treatment, ensuring compliance with safety standards
Masonry and wood construction with incombustible exterior walls, providing a balance of materials
Steel, iron, concrete, or masonry construction — incombustible throughout
Fire-resistive construction with maximum rating for structural elements, which is crucial for high-risk areas

questions.rationale: Type II = wood with 1-hr fire-resistive treatment. Type III = masonry and wood (incombustible exterior). Type IV = steel/iron/concrete/masonry (incombustible throughout, non-bearing may use treated wood). Type V = fire-resistive (highest rating).

questions.text: A 5-storey shopping mall in Cebu City is constructed of reinforced concrete with a fire-resistive structural system. Under PD 1096, what are the correct Occupancy Group and Construction Type?

options.text: Group M (Mercantile), Type I
Group E (Business and Mercantile), Type V
Group C (Education and Recreation), Type IV
Group E (Business and Mercantile), Type I

questions.rationale: This question combines two traps: (1) Group M is a US IBC label, not PD 1096 — the PH code uses Group E; (2) Type I in PD 1096 means wood construction, not the most fire-resistive type as in some US systems.

questions.text: Under Rule X, Section 1005, what is the minimum vertical clearance for a CANOPY (marquee) above pavement?
questions.rationale: Canopy (permanent marquee) = 3.00 m + 2-hr fire-resistive, incombustible. Awning (movable) = 2.40 m, no specific fire rating. Both must be at least 300 mm from the curb.

questions.text: A firewall is required to achieve a 3-hour fire-resistive occupancy separation between a warehouse and a condominium sharing a common wall. The wall is 20.00 m long. A building manager requests a 12.00 m² double door opening and a 4.00 m² service window. Are these openings compliant per PD 1096, Rule XII, Section 1204?

options.text: Yes — the total opening (16.00 m²) is less than 25% of the wall area
No — the 12.00 m² double door exceeds the maximum single opening of 10.00 m²
Yes — as long as 3-hour fire assemblies are installed at both openings
No — no openings are permitted in a 3-hour occupancy separation wall under any circumstances

questions.rationale: The two limits operate independently: the 25%-of-length limit controls total opening width, while the 10.00 m² single-opening cap prevents any individual penetration from being so large that it defeats the wall's fire-separation function. A 4.00 m² service window alone would be compliant; the 12.00 m² door is the violation.

questions.text: Under PD 1096 Sec. 603, what is the minimum concrete cover required over the reinforcing steel in a reinforced concrete floor slab designed for a 1-hour fire resistance rating?

options.text: 10 millimeters of concrete cover over the main reinforcement
15 millimeters of concrete cover over the main reinforcement
20 millimeters of concrete cover over the main reinforcement
25 millimeters of concrete cover over the main reinforcement

questions.rationale: Sec. 603 specifies concrete cover requirements for RC slabs by fire resistance rating: 15mm for 1-hour, 20mm for 2-hour, 25mm for 3-hour, and 25mm for 4-hour ratings.
questions.explanation: The 15mm cover for 1-hour rating is the minimum; it protects reinforcing steel from reaching the critical temperature at which steel loses structural capacity. Increasing cover increases fire resistance because concrete is a poor thermal conductor, delaying heat transfer to the steel.

questions.text: Under PD 1096 Sec. 603, a 4-hour fire-rated RC column must have what minimum cross-sectional dimension AND what minimum concrete cover over the main reinforcement?

options.text: 400mm column dimension with 40mm concrete cover over main bars
450mm column dimension with 50mm concrete cover over main bars
450mm column dimension with 25mm concrete cover over main bars
500mm column dimension with 40mm concrete cover over main bars

questions.rationale: For a 4-hour rating, Sec. 603 requires a minimum RC column dimension of 450mm. The RC slab cover table shows 25mm for both 3-hour and 4-hour ratings — the column dimension (not increased cover) provides the additional fire resistance at the 4-hour level.
questions.explanation: This question tests whether candidates conflate slab cover with column cover requirements. The 450mm column dimension for 4-hour rating is the critical differentiator from the 400mm 3-hour column. The 25mm cover applies to slabs (same for 3-hour and 4-hour). Column fire resistance at the highest levels is achieved primarily through mass, not cover alone.

questions.text: What minimum slab thickness does PD 1096 require for a reinforced concrete floor slab to achieve a 2-hour fire resistance rating?

options.text: 75 millimeters minimum slab thickness
100 millimeters minimum slab thickness
125 millimeters minimum slab thickness
150 millimeters minimum slab thickness

questions.rationale: Sec. 603 sets RC slab thickness requirements by fire rating: 100mm for 1-hour, 125mm for 2-hour, 150mm for 3-hour, and 150mm for 4-hour ratings.
questions.explanation: The 125mm threshold for 2-hour rating reflects the increased thermal mass needed to slow heat transmission through the slab. Note that 3-hour and 4-hour ratings share the same 150mm minimum thickness — the additional cover requirements differentiate them at higher ratings.

questions.text: A steel column must achieve a 2-hour fire resistance rating using spray-applied mineral fiber protection. What minimum thickness of protection does PD 1096 require?

options.text: 12 millimeters of spray-applied mineral fiber protection
20 millimeters of spray-applied mineral fiber protection
38 millimeters of spray-applied mineral fiber protection
50 millimeters of spray-applied mineral fiber protection

questions.rationale: Sec. 603 specifies metal protection (spray-applied mineral fiber or plaster) thicknesses: 12mm for 1-hour, 20mm for 2-hour, 38mm for 3-hour, and 50mm for 4-hour ratings.
questions.explanation: The 20mm minimum for a 2-hour rating applies to the applied protection layer, measured from the steel surface. The progressive increase from 12mm to 50mm reflects the thermal resistance needed to keep steel below its critical temperature (approximately 550°C) for the rated duration.

questions.text: A 4-hour fire-rated steel column requires spray-applied mineral fiber protection. The contractor proposes using 38mm of protection instead of the code-required minimum. How does this affect compliance?

options.text: 38mm complies because it exceeds the 20mm minimum for 2-hour protection
38mm does not comply; it meets only the 3-hour minimum of 38mm, not the 4-hour minimum of 50mm
38mm complies because spray fiber is more effective than gypsum plaster at equivalent thickness
38mm does not comply; the minimum for any fire-rated steel protection is 50mm regardless of rating

questions.rationale: Sec. 603 requires 50mm of spray-applied protection for a 4-hour rating. The contractor's proposed 38mm satisfies only the 3-hour minimum. A 4-hour rated assembly requires the full 50mm thickness.
questions.explanation: This scenario tests reading the correct row from the protection thickness table. 38mm is not random — it is a legitimate code value (for 3-hour rating), which makes it a plausible error. The 50mm requirement for 4-hour protection is the critical boundary. Inspectors must verify actual applied thickness, not just material specification.

questions.text: The Philippine Fire Mechanical and Electrical Code (PFMEC) classifies building components into categories that determine fire resistance requirements. Which building type in the Philippine system represents the LEAST fire-resistive construction category?

options.text: Type I, which requires the highest fire resistance because it is numbered first
Type I, which represents the least fire-resistive construction in the Philippine system
Type V, which represents the least fire-resistive construction in the Philippine system
Type III, which is the midpoint and therefore represents ordinary construction

questions.rationale: In the Philippine system under PD 1096, Type I is the least fire-resistive construction type. This is the opposite of the International Building Code (IBC) convention, where Type I is the most fire-resistive.
questions.explanation: Philippine LEA candidates frequently confuse the local Type I-V system with the IBC system. In PD 1096, Type I = least fire-resistive (wood frame, combustible) and Type V = most fire-resistive (fire-resistive construction). The IBC numbers in the opposite direction. Memorizing this reversal is essential for LEA preparation.

questions.text: A prestressed concrete floor member requires a 3-hour fire resistance rating. What minimum concrete cover over the prestressing tendons does PD 1096 require?

options.text: 25 millimeters of cover over the prestressing tendons
40 millimeters of cover over the prestressing tendons
50 millimeters of cover over the prestressing tendons
65 millimeters of cover over the prestressing tendons

questions.rationale: Sec. 603 specifies prestressed concrete cover requirements: 25mm for 1-hour, 40mm for 2-hour, 50mm for 3-hour, and 65mm for 4-hour ratings. Prestressed tendons require more cover than mild steel because they lose tensile strength at lower temperatures.
questions.explanation: Prestressing tendons (high-strength steel wire or strand) are more sensitive to elevated temperatures than conventional mild steel reinforcement. They begin losing significant tensile strength at around 300°C, versus 500°C for mild steel. This is why prestressed members require substantially greater cover — 50mm vs. 25mm at the 3-hour level.

questions.text: What is the minimum cross-sectional dimension of a reinforced concrete column required to achieve a 3-hour fire resistance rating under PD 1096?

options.text: 200 millimeters minimum column dimension
300 millimeters minimum column dimension
400 millimeters minimum column dimension
450 millimeters minimum column dimension

questions.rationale: Sec. 603 specifies RC column minimum dimensions by fire rating: 200mm for 1-hour, 300mm for 2-hour, 400mm for 3-hour, and 450mm for 4-hour ratings.
questions.explanation: The 400mm minimum dimension for 3-hour rating ensures that even if the outer concrete spalls during a fire, sufficient protected concrete core remains around the reinforcing steel to maintain structural integrity. Column dimensions govern independently of cover requirements.

questions.text: An architect specifies a prestressed concrete beam with 40mm cover and a 125mm slab depth for a floor system. A building inspector claims this meets a 2-hour fire rating for the beam. Is the inspector correct, and which code provision governs?

options.text: Correct: 40mm cover satisfies the 2-hour prestressed requirement and 125mm slab satisfies the 2-hour slab depth
Incorrect: 40mm cover satisfies 2-hour prestressed beams, but the slab must be 150mm for a combined 2-hour assembly
Incorrect: 40mm cover is only the 2-hour requirement for RC slabs, not prestressed members which need 50mm
Correct: 40mm cover for any concrete member and 125mm minimum slab depth together achieve a 2-hour assembly

questions.rationale: Sec. 603 specifies 40mm cover for 2-hour prestressed concrete members and 125mm minimum slab thickness for 2-hour RC slabs. Both specifications are satisfied, making the inspector's assessment correct.
questions.explanation: This question requires simultaneous application of two separate Sec. 603 tables: the prestressed member cover table (40mm = 2-hour) and the RC slab thickness table (125mm = 2-hour). Both conditions are independently satisfied at the 2-hour level. The distractor in option B uses the 3-hour slab thickness (150mm), testing whether candidates can distinguish between the two fire rating levels.

questions.text: A concrete masonry unit (CMU) partition wall must achieve a 2-hour fire resistance rating. Comparing the required partition thickness to the 1-hour requirement, which statement correctly describes the code relationship?

options.text: The 2-hour wall requires exactly double the thickness of the 1-hour wall, which is a common misconception as fire resistance does not scale linearly
The 2-hour wall requires a proportionally larger thickness increase than the step from 2-hour to 3-hour, due to the nonlinear behavior of materials under fire conditions
The partition thickness scales linearly with fire rating from 1-hour through 4-hour, which is not accurate as material properties affect the scaling
The thickness increments between adjacent fire ratings are not constant because material behavior is nonlinear

questions.rationale: Sec. 603 partition thickness requirements reflect the nonlinear relationship between wall mass and fire resistance duration. Each rating step does not produce a proportional thickness increase because heat transfer through masonry is a time-dependent, nonlinear process.
questions.explanation: Fire resistance testing of masonry walls shows diminishing returns at higher ratings — a wall twice as thick does not provide twice the fire resistance. The code tables reflect tested values, not calculated proportions. This explains why RC slab thicknesses plateau (both 3-hour and 4-hour require 150mm) while cover requirements continue to increase.

questions.text: Under PD 1096 Sec. 603, a 4-hour fire-rated RC column must have what minimum cross-sectional dimension AND what minimum concrete cover over the main reinforcement?

options.text: 400mm column dimension with 40mm concrete cover over main bars
450mm column dimension with 50mm concrete cover over main bars
450mm column dimension with 25mm concrete cover over main bars
500mm column dimension with 40mm concrete cover over main bars

questions.rationale: For a 4-hour rating, Sec. 603 requires a minimum RC column dimension of 450mm. The RC slab cover table shows 25mm for both 3-hour and 4-hour ratings — the column dimension (not increased cover) provides the additional fire resistance at the 4-hour level.
questions.explanation: This question tests whether candidates conflate slab cover with column cover requirements. The 450mm column dimension for 4-hour rating is the critical differentiator from the 400mm 3-hour column. The 25mm cover applies to slabs (same for 3-hour and 4-hour). Column fire resistance at the highest levels is achieved primarily through mass, not cover alone.

questions.text: A 4-hour fire-rated steel column requires spray-applied mineral fiber protection. The contractor proposes using 38mm of protection instead of the code-required minimum. How does this affect compliance?

options.text: 38mm complies because it exceeds the 20mm minimum for 2-hour protection
38mm does not comply; it meets only the 3-hour minimum of 38mm, not the 4-hour minimum of 50mm
38mm complies because spray fiber is more effective than gypsum plaster at equivalent thickness
38mm does not comply; the minimum for any fire-rated steel protection is 50mm regardless of rating

questions.rationale: Sec. 603 requires 50mm of spray-applied protection for a 4-hour rating. The contractor's proposed 38mm satisfies only the 3-hour minimum. A 4-hour rated assembly requires the full 50mm thickness.
questions.explanation: This scenario tests reading the correct row from the protection thickness table. 38mm is not random — it is a legitimate code value (for 3-hour rating), which makes it a plausible error. The 50mm requirement for 4-hour protection is the critical boundary. Inspectors must verify actual applied thickness, not just material specification.

questions.text: An architect specifies a prestressed concrete beam with 40mm cover and a 125mm slab depth for a floor system. A building inspector claims this meets a 2-hour fire rating for the beam. Is the inspector correct, and which code provision governs?

options.text: Correct: 40mm cover satisfies the 2-hour prestressed requirement and 125mm slab satisfies the 2-hour slab depth
Incorrect: 40mm cover satisfies 2-hour prestressed beams, but the slab must be 150mm for a combined 2-hour assembly
Incorrect: 40mm cover is only the 2-hour requirement for RC slabs, not prestressed members which need 50mm
Correct: 40mm cover for any concrete member and 125mm minimum slab depth together achieve a 2-hour assembly

questions.rationale: Sec. 603 specifies 40mm cover for 2-hour prestressed concrete members and 125mm minimum slab thickness for 2-hour RC slabs. Both specifications are satisfied, making the inspector's assessment correct.
questions.explanation: This question requires simultaneous application of two separate Sec. 603 tables: the prestressed member cover table (40mm = 2-hour) and the RC slab thickness table (125mm = 2-hour). Both conditions are independently satisfied at the 2-hour level. The distractor in option B uses the 3-hour slab thickness (150mm), testing whether candidates can distinguish between the two fire rating levels.

questions.text: Under PD 1096 Sec. 603, what is the minimum concrete cover required over the reinforcing steel in a reinforced concrete floor slab designed for a 1-hour fire resistance rating?

options.text: 10 millimeters of concrete cover over the main reinforcement
15 millimeters of concrete cover over the main reinforcement
20 millimeters of concrete cover over the main reinforcement
25 millimeters of concrete cover over the main reinforcement

questions.rationale: Sec. 603 specifies concrete cover requirements for RC slabs by fire resistance rating: 15mm for 1-hour, 20mm for 2-hour, 25mm for 3-hour, and 25mm for 4-hour ratings.
questions.explanation: The 15mm cover for 1-hour rating is the minimum; it protects reinforcing steel from reaching the critical temperature at which steel loses structural capacity. Increasing cover increases fire resistance because concrete is a poor thermal conductor, delaying heat transfer to the steel.

questions.text: The Philippine Fire Mechanical and Electrical Code (PFMEC) classifies building components into categories that determine fire resistance requirements. Which building type in the Philippine system represents the LEAST fire-resistive construction category?

options.text: Type I, which requires the highest fire resistance because it is numbered first
Type I, which represents the least fire-resistive construction in the Philippine system
Type V, which represents the least fire-resistive construction in the Philippine system
Type III, which is the midpoint and therefore represents ordinary construction

questions.rationale: In the Philippine system under PD 1096, Type I is the least fire-resistive construction type. This is the opposite of the International Building Code (IBC) convention, where Type I is the most fire-resistive.
questions.explanation: Philippine LEA candidates frequently confuse the local Type I-V system with the IBC system. In PD 1096, Type I = least fire-resistive (wood frame, combustible) and Type V = most fire-resistive (fire-resistive construction). The IBC numbers in the opposite direction. Memorizing this reversal is essential for LEA preparation.

questions.text: A prestressed concrete floor member requires a 3-hour fire resistance rating. What minimum concrete cover over the prestressing tendons does PD 1096 require?

options.text: 25 millimeters of cover over the prestressing tendons
40 millimeters of cover over the prestressing tendons
50 millimeters of cover over the prestressing tendons
65 millimeters of cover over the prestressing tendons

questions.rationale: Sec. 603 specifies prestressed concrete cover requirements: 25mm for 1-hour, 40mm for 2-hour, 50mm for 3-hour, and 65mm for 4-hour ratings. Prestressed tendons require more cover than mild steel because they lose tensile strength at lower temperatures.
questions.explanation: Prestressing tendons (high-strength steel wire or strand) are more sensitive to elevated temperatures than conventional mild steel reinforcement. They begin losing significant tensile strength at around 300°C, versus 500°C for mild steel. This is why prestressed members require substantially greater cover — 50mm vs. 25mm at the 3-hour level.

questions.text: What minimum slab thickness does PD 1096 require for a reinforced concrete floor slab to achieve a 2-hour fire resistance rating?

options.text: 75 millimeters minimum slab thickness
100 millimeters minimum slab thickness
125 millimeters minimum slab thickness
150 millimeters minimum slab thickness

questions.rationale: Sec. 603 sets RC slab thickness requirements by fire rating: 100mm for 1-hour, 125mm for 2-hour, 150mm for 3-hour, and 150mm for 4-hour ratings.
questions.explanation: The 125mm threshold for 2-hour rating reflects the increased thermal mass needed to slow heat transmission through the slab. Note that 3-hour and 4-hour ratings share the same 150mm minimum thickness — the additional cover requirements differentiate them at higher ratings.

questions.text: A steel column must achieve a 2-hour fire resistance rating using spray-applied mineral fiber protection. What minimum thickness of protection does PD 1096 require?

options.text: 12 millimeters of spray-applied mineral fiber protection
20 millimeters of spray-applied mineral fiber protection
38 millimeters of spray-applied mineral fiber protection
50 millimeters of spray-applied mineral fiber protection

questions.rationale: Sec. 603 specifies metal protection (spray-applied mineral fiber or plaster) thicknesses: 12mm for 1-hour, 20mm for 2-hour, 38mm for 3-hour, and 50mm for 4-hour ratings.
questions.explanation: The 20mm minimum for a 2-hour rating applies to the applied protection layer, measured from the steel surface. The progressive increase from 12mm to 50mm reflects the thermal resistance needed to keep steel below its critical temperature (approximately 550°C) for the rated duration.

questions.text: A concrete masonry unit (CMU) partition wall must achieve a 2-hour fire resistance rating. Comparing the required partition thickness to the 1-hour requirement, which statement correctly describes the code relationship?

options.text: The 2-hour wall requires exactly double the thickness of the 1-hour wall, assuming uniform material properties and consistent environmental conditions
The 2-hour wall requires a proportionally larger thickness increase than the step from 2-hour to 3-hour, due to nonlinear scaling of fire resistance properties
The partition thickness scales linearly with fire rating from 1-hour through 4-hour, based on standard industry assumptions and typical material performance
The thickness increments between adjacent fire ratings are not constant because material behavior is nonlinear

questions.rationale: Sec. 603 partition thickness requirements reflect the nonlinear relationship between wall mass and fire resistance duration. Each rating step does not produce a proportional thickness increase because heat transfer through masonry is a time-dependent, nonlinear process.
questions.explanation: Fire resistance testing of masonry walls shows diminishing returns at higher ratings — a wall twice as thick does not provide twice the fire resistance. The code tables reflect tested values, not calculated proportions. This explains why RC slab thicknesses plateau (both 3-hour and 4-hour require 150mm) while cover requirements continue to increase.

questions.text: What is the minimum cross-sectional dimension of a reinforced concrete column required to achieve a 3-hour fire resistance rating under PD 1096?

options.text: 200 millimeters minimum column dimension
300 millimeters minimum column dimension
400 millimeters minimum column dimension
450 millimeters minimum column dimension

questions.rationale: Sec. 603 specifies RC column minimum dimensions by fire rating: 200mm for 1-hour, 300mm for 2-hour, 400mm for 3-hour, and 450mm for 4-hour ratings.
questions.explanation: The 400mm minimum dimension for 3-hour rating ensures that even if the outer concrete spalls during a fire, sufficient protected concrete core remains around the reinforcing steel to maintain structural integrity. Column dimensions govern independently of cover requirements.
